Nullity means the state of being absolutely nothing — not just unimportant or weak, but having no existence, no power, and no effect whatsoever. It is the noun form of "null," which means zero, void, or nonexistent. A "nullity" is therefore either the condition of having no force, value, or validity, or something (an act, a rule, a person) that is entirely without effect or consequence — something that amounts to nothing.
The legal meaning (most important and most common)

This is where "nullity" lives most precisely and is used most often.

In law, a nullity is an act, agreement, or proceeding that is considered to have never been legally valid — not just cancelled or ended, but treated as though it never legally existed in the first place. This is a crucial distinction. When something is cancelled, it was once valid and has now been brought to an end. When something is a nullity, it was never valid to begin with. The law looks back at it and says: this never counted.

Example: If someone signs a contract while being threatened or forced, a court can declare that contract a nullity. This means it has no legal force and both parties are placed back in the position they were in before, as if the contract was never made.

Marriage nullity is one of the most widely known applications. A declaration of nullity (sometimes called an annulment) is a court's official ruling that a marriage was legally invalid from the very start. It is importantly different from a divorce. A divorce ends a marriage that was valid. A declaration of nullity says the marriage was never legally real to begin with — perhaps because one person was already married to someone else, or was underage, or lacked the mental capacity to genuinely consent.

Within legal nullity, there is a further distinction worth knowing. An act or marriage that is void is automatically a nullity — it has no legal effect from the very moment it was supposedly made, without anyone needing to go to court to say so. A voidable act, on the other hand, is treated as valid until a court formally declares it a nullity. The difference matters practically: a void act is a nullity by its very nature, while a voidable act only becomes one upon a court's declaration. Until that declaration happens, a voidable act holds.

Outside of law, "nullity" is used more broadly to describe anything — an act, a statement, a ruling, a person — that is entirely without effect, importance, or consequence. It amounts to nothing.

"The committee's decision was a complete nullity — the board overruled it within the hour."

"Despite his grand pronouncements, his authority in that room was a nullity."

Calling something a nullity in everyday language is a pointed, dismissive statement. You are not just saying it is weak or unimportant. You are saying it carries no weight, produces no result, and might as well not exist. It is one of the stronger ways in English to express that something is utterly without value or consequence.

"Nullity" can also refer to a person who is a complete nonentity — someone with no power, no influence, and no significance in a given situation. This usage is formal and literary, so you will encounter it in writing more than in everyday speech.

In mathematics, specifically in linear algebra, nullity has a precise technical meaning.

When you have a matrix (a rectangular grid of numbers that represents a mathematical transformation — a rule for turning one set of values into another), its null space is the collection of all input vectors that the transformation maps to zero. In other words: all the inputs that, when fed into the transformation, produce an output of zero.

The nullity of a matrix is the dimension of that null space — essentially, the "size" of the collection of inputs that all collapse to zero.

Here is why it matters: the rank-nullity theorem is a foundational result in linear algebra that says, for any matrix with n columns, its rank (roughly, the amount of meaningful, independent information it carries) plus its nullity must always equal n. So nullity tells you how much "information is lost" when the transformation is applied. A high nullity means many different inputs all produce the same zero output, so the transformation is destroying a lot of information. A nullity of zero means no information is lost — every distinct input produces a distinct output — and the transformation is called injective (one-to-one).
The common thread across all meanings

Whether you encounter "nullity" in law, in everyday speech, or in mathematics, it always carries the same underlying idea: the complete absence of force, validity, or effect. Something that is a nullity does not merely fail or fall short — it is as if it never happened, never existed, or never had any power to begin with. It is the strongest possible statement that something counts for nothing.
